title: Sample-based quantum simulation of vibrational structure of polyyne chains
authors: Sarah Mostame, Tanvi P. Gujarati, Alberto Baiardi, Abhijit Mitra, Dimitar Trenev, Sumathy Raman
abstract: Predicting anharmonic vibrational spectra is a complex computational task, which becomes quickly infeasible as molecular size and the number of vibrational basis functions increase, leading to an exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. Here, we employ a sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) framework to compute anharmonic vibrational energies and spectra. The approach combines quantum state preparation and sampling with configuration recovery, diagonalization of the Hamiltonian projected in a subspace of basis configurations, and calculation of transition-dipole moments to obtain both vibrational energies and infrared spectra. We investigate two approaches for sampling, namely, vib-LUCJ and vib-SqDRIFT and apply the method to study the polyyne molecules C$_2$H$_2$ and C$_4$H$_2$, reaching representations requiring up to 104 qubits. Beyond energies, transition-dipole calculations reveal that infrared intensities and excited-state composition continue to evolve with basis size through anharmonic mixing and intensity redistribution, even when low-energy eigenvalues appear converged. These results show that sample-based quantum subspace methods can capture spectroscopic information in vibrational spaces far beyond the regime of full diagonalization. Moreover, our simulation identify multi-state recovery and scalable projected-space treatment as central challenges for further scaling sample-based approaches.
summary: This paper introduces a Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) method to calculate the complex anharmonic vibrational spectra of polyynes. By projecting the massive vibrational Hamiltonian onto a small, sampled subspace, the authors overcome the exponential scaling problem. The results demonstrate that this quantum approach can accurately predict both vibrational energies and sensitive spectroscopic details, like infrared intensities.
main_problem: The core challenge is predicting anharmonic vibrational spectra, which is computationally infeasible due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space with molecular size.
main_result: The sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) framework successfully computes vibrational energies and spectroscopic observables for polyynes in subspaces far smaller than the full theoretical space.
method: The authors employ an end-to-end SQD framework combining quantum state preparation (using vib-LUCJ or vib-SqDRIFT ansatze), configuration recovery, and diagonalization projected onto a selected subspace.
model_or_system: The study focuses on polyyne chains (C2H2 and C4H2) whose anharmonic vibrational Hamiltonian is modeled using a multi-mode expansion. The electronic structure calculations are based on DFT (B3LYP/def2-SVP).
key_observables: Vibrational energies, infrared spectra, and transition-dipole moments (which determine intensities and excited-state composition).
important_parameters: The system size is quantified by the Hilbert space dimension, which can reach $\approx 5.5 \times 10^{11}$ for C4H2.
main_assumptions: The primary limitations noted are the need for systematic optimization of sampling parameters and the fact that spectroscopic observables are more sensitive than ground-state energies.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the modal representation and qubit encoding. Other figures compare SQD results for transition dipole moments ($0 \to m$ transitions) against exact diagonalization for C2H2 and C4H2.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of anharmonic spectra. It then details the SQD framework, comparing two sampling strategies (vib-LUCJ and vib-SqDRIFT) to calculate energies and, critically, transition-dipole moments, concluding with resource estimates for quantum implementation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the simulation of molecular vibrations, a core topic in AMO physics, by developing a quantum algorithm to circumvent the exponential scaling inherent in full diagonalization of the vibrational Hamiltonian.
